strengths: Clear and well-motivated system contribution: Lumos-1 keeps a standard Llama-style architecture with minimal modification while achieving competitive autoregressive video generation, avoiding external text encoders and next-token decoding latency.

MM-RoPE is supported by a thoughtful diagnostic analysis (frequency spectrum imbalance in 3D RoPE, aliasing/rotation-speed visualization in Fig. 3) and a reasonably thorough ablation over the number of meta components and scaling factors (Figs. 7, 9).

AR-DF is well designed: the temporal tube masking to combat spatial information leakage is motivated by frame-wise validation loss analysis (Fig. 7a), and the train–inference masking consistency issue is identified and addressed with a compatible inference scheme and sensitivity analysis of the inference mask ratio (Fig. 8).

Impressive resource efficiency: pre-training from scratch on 60M images / 10M videos with only 48 GPUs while matching EMU3 on GenEval and COSMOS-Video2World on VBench-I2V is a meaningful result for reproducibility and democratization.

Comprehensive ablation studies (tube masks, MM-RoPE components, CFG scale, aspect-ratio robustness, inference overhead in Table 4) and detailed implementation/appendix material increase reproducibility; code and models are stated to be released.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix D), including modest data scale and societal impact safeguards.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: MM-RoPE is a channel-rearrangement and scaling variant of existing 3D RoPE / M-RoPE, and AR-DF essentially combines Diffusion Forcing with VideoMAE-style tube masking; each component builds closely on prior techniques, and the theoretical grounding is limited to empirical validation-loss evidence rather than generation-quality ablations at scale for some design choices.

The 'unified model perspective' claim is weakened: the language modeling loss is removed during training (only visual logits), and no language understanding or generation capability is evaluated, so the model is effectively a visual generator with text conditioning rather than a demonstrated unified model.

Primary evaluation relies on GenEval and (partial) VBench metrics; no FVD, no human evaluation, and VBench tables omit several metrics 'due to space limits', which weakens the strength of the video quality claims. The claim of being 'on par with FLUX' based on a single GenEval point (0.664 vs 0.67) is somewhat overstated.

Comparisons are to models trained with far more data/compute, and several strong recent autoregressive video baselines are cited but not compared quantitatively; the efficiency advantage of discrete diffusion inference over EMU3-style next-token decoding is asserted but not quantified with an end-to-end latency/throughput table.

Key hyperparameters (mask ratios, scaling factor (4,8,8), 2:3:3 channel ratio, ρinf=0.7) are largely empirical, with limited analysis of why these values transfer across model scales; the 0.5B model is used for most ablations, leaving open whether findings hold for the 3B model.

Presentation issues remain: typos ('pre-tarin', 'classier-free guidance'), confusing figure annotations and duplicated layer artifacts in Fig. 5, and some notation (Eq. 5 indices) is hard to parse, suggesting the manuscript was not fully polished.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: unifying autoregressive video generation with standard LLM architectures without external text encoders, and the design choices (intra-frame bidirectionality + inter-frame temporal causality) are well-motivated by the structure of video data.

MM-RoPE is supported by a careful diagnostic analysis (frequency allocation, aliasing due to low-frequency channels for spatial positions), and the design is incremental but clearly reasoned; ablations on the number of meta components and scaling factors are fairly thorough.

AR-DF's temporal tube masking is a sensible fix for information leakage in temporally-causal masked prediction, and the frame-wise loss analysis (Figure 7a) provides intuitive evidence for the claimed shortcut problem.

The resource efficiency claim is notable: pre-training from scratch on 48 GPUs and achieving results in the vicinity of much larger systems (EMU3 8B, COSMOS-Video2World 5B+11B) is a useful data point.
The paper includes implementation details (memory-friendly loss, stage-wise training, sequence formatting), a detailed inference algorithm, and stated plans to release code and models.
weaknesses: Results are only 'comparable' to baselines rather than better: the paper is positioned against much larger and more resource-intensive models, and its headline claim rests on parity with EMU3/COSMOS/OpenSoraPlan rather than any clear quantitative or qualitative win. At a top venue, this is a thin contribution proposition.

Novelty is limited. MM-RoPE is an incremental refinement of M-RoPE, RoPE-2D, TAD-RoPE, and VideoRoPE (all cited), and AR-DF is essentially temporal tube masking (from VideoMAE) applied to diffusion forcing; the training/inference asymmetry handled by inference-time masking is a somewhat awkward patch rather than a principled solution, and the authors concede the position scaling 'may not be the optimal solution'.

Most ablations are evaluated only via validation cross-entropy loss at 0.5B scale. The claimed correlation between loss and generation quality is assumed (citing prior work), never demonstrated; several design decisions (e.g., MM-RoPE default of 4 meta components, scaling (4,8,8)) would need end-task metric or human evaluation support.

Evaluation has fairness and rigor concerns: GenEval scores are obtained after rewriting prompts with Qwen 32B (guidance scale 16), which can inflate alignment scores; VBench comparisons are 'partial metrics due to space limits'; no FVD, no human evaluation, and no statistical variance reported. The claim of being 'on par with FLUX' overstates what 0.664 vs 0.67 on GenEval supports.

Generation scope is narrow: 25 frames, resolutions around 448x256/672x384, and a modest data regime the authors themselves acknowledge under-generalizes. Long-video capability, which motivates the autoregressive design, is not evaluated at all.

The inference scheme requires re-masking a fixed ratio (rho_inf=0.7) of tokens in each generated frame before caching, and the paper shows quality is highly sensitive to this ratio and degrades without it - a notable practical weakness of AR-DF that is downplayed.

Comparisons mix configurations in ways that are hard to parse (different resolutions/aspect ratios across tables; Table 2 reports a 3.6B model labeled '1.5B' parameter row; Table B1 lists 'Lumos-1 1B' as 1.5B params), raising questions about which configuration produced which number.

Writing quality is below the bar for a top venue: typos ('pre-tarin', 'classier-free guidance', 'Stabel Diffusion', 'factorsinMM-RoPE'), inconsistent naming (EMU3 vs EMU-3, COSMOS-Video2World citation mismatched to Cosmos [1]), and figure artifacts (placeholder text visible in figures 2, 4, 5, 6, 8) suggest a rushed submission.

The efficiency story is only partially substantiated: inference latency comparisons exist for RoPE variants (Table 4), but there is no systematic inference-cost comparison against the diffusion baselines despite the 'prohibitive latency' motivation; the 50-step per-frame generation with CFG seems expensive and is not benchmarked against alternatives.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: building an autoregressive video generator that stays compatible with standard LLM architectures (no external text encoder, discrete diffusion inference) addresses a real gap in the unified-model literature.

Two concrete technical contributions: (1) MM-RoPE, with a well-diagnosed limitation of vanilla 3D RoPE (imbalanced frequency spectra across temporal/spatial channels) and a principled distributed+scaled design; (2) AR-DF, which identifies the frame-wise loss imbalance caused by spatial information leakage under temporal causality and addresses it with temporal tube masking plus a matched inference-time masking policy.

The analysis is unusually thorough: the frequency-spectrum visualization (Fig. 3b/3c), the meta MM-RoPE count ablation, and the scaling-factor ablation provide concrete evidence for design choices rather than just asserting them.

The AR-DF ablations (frame-wise validation loss with random vs. tube masks, sensitivity of inference mask ratio) directly support the claimed mechanism (information leakage vs. genuine temporal propagation), which strengthens the paper's causal narrative.

Impressive efficiency: training from scratch on only 48 GPUs with 60M images/10M videos and achieving GenEval/VBench results comparable to EMU3, COSMOS-Video2World, and OpenSoraPlan is a meaningful practical contribution; memory-friendly techniques (chunked cross-entropy, flash attention) are useful implementation details.
Code and model release, detailed inference algorithms (Algo. 2/3), and appendix coverage of sequence formatting, training hyperparameters, limitations, and societal impact support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: MM-RoPE builds directly on M-RoPE (Qwen2-VL) with re-allocation of channels and position scaling, and AR-DF is essentially diffusion forcing (Chen et al.) combined with temporal tube masking (VideoMAE) applied to a discrete AR setting. The paper positions itself against these works but the conceptual delta is modest.

Key ablations (MM-RoPE, meta counts, scaling factors, tube masks) are validated only via validation cross-entropy loss at 0.5B scale; there is no end-to-end evidence that these loss improvements translate to better final generation metrics (GenEval/VBench/FVD) at full scale, so the central claims about generation quality rest partly on a proxy metric.

Benchmark comparisons are not strictly apples-to-apples: Lumos-1 results at different resolutions (352x352 for GenEval, 448x256x25 for T2V, 672x384x25 for I2V) are compared against baselines at different resolutions and data scales, and the 'comparable' framing may be inflated; caption rewriting with Qwen 32B on GenEval also introduces a confound relative to baselines' pipelines.

Some claimed efficiencies are asserted rather than benchmarked: the discrete-diffusion inference efficiency advantage over EMU3 is stated qualitatively, and Table 4 only shows latency overhead of RoPE variants, not comparisons with competing AR/diffusion video generators.

Presentation is not yet polished: leftover draft artifacts appear in figures (e.g., Chinese working notes '视频自回归模型 (LlamaVGen)', 'V3（暂定，合并两个图）' in Fig. 2/5), typos ('pre-tarin', 'classier-free guidance'), and some figures/tables list partial metrics with missing baseline entries.

Scalability of the proposed designs is uncertain: all full-scale results use 10M videos with limited resolution (25 frames, ≤672x384), and the paper acknowledges weak generalization on intricate dynamics; the strongest competing systems were trained on 10-100x more data, making scaling behavior of MM-RoPE/AR-DF an open question.

Missing baselines/analyses: no comparison with other recent micro-AR video methods (e.g., Loong, VideoMAR, GameGen-X style models) on the same benchmarks, no FVD on standard video suites, and no human evaluation to complement VBench.
